## The Art of the Dull: Photography Philosophy Heats Up

The conversation on 4chan’s /p/ board has shifted from technical specs to aesthetic philosophy, driven largely by the persistent critic known as user cANON. In a lengthy critique, cANON labeled street photography the "dullest franchise" in the medium, citing clichéd juxtapositions, relentless black-and-white gloom, and uninspired subjects like puddles and hobos. The debate was sparked by a post noting that Elliot Rodger’s father exhibited his photos as "Fine Art," prompting a broader discussion on whether photography qualifies as art at all.

While some users mocked cANON for lacking the "fruits of intelligence" or speculated on his Iranian or Serbian heritage based on his posting style, the core argument holds weight: photographic quality, rather than camera specifications, should dictate the value of one's equipment. This sentiment crystallized into a new board motto: "gear only matters if your photo doesn't suck." Users agreed that compositional skill is secondary to no one, marking a collective groan at the endless gear threads that have long dominated the community.

## Mirrorless Wars: Sony vs. The Rest

On the /gear/ board, the mirrorless debate remains fierce, with users weighing the merits of Sony, Nikon, and Panasonic. The consensus suggests that video requirements are increasingly diminishing the experience for pure photo enthusiasts. One user advocated for the Panasonic S5 and the L-Mount alliance due to superior video codecs and better Sigma lens compatibility. Others defended the Nikon Z7II for its robust adapter support and native lens quality.

Sony, often the default choice, faced criticism for being a "slightly worse Nikon" that commands a premium, with specific models like the A5000 dismissed for lacking an EVF. Meanwhile, Panasonic was teased for noisy fans and "half-assed" photo features compared to its video prowess. A recurring tension exists between photographers and videographers, with Panasonic users pejoratively referred to as "videofags" by purists who favor EF and PL lens compatibility. Despite the toxicity and echo-chamber complaints, many defended /gear/ as functional compared to other boards, provided you ignore the "Canon" users who start conflicts and get humiliated.

## Botanical Details and Social Cringe

In a quieter corner of /p/, the "Recent Photos Thread" highlighted the community’s appreciation for natural detail. A highly detailed close-up of glossy green foliage with strong sunlight highlights sparked discussions about whether the image was taken during local "tram races," linking static images to specific events.

Conversely, the social dynamics of street photography were scrutinized. Users debated the "cringe" factor when approaching strangers, wondering why subjects often get defensive. The consensus pointed to the psychological barrier of intrusion; while photographers view their craft as benign, subjects often feel their private moments are being captured without permission, leading to natural self-defense rather than rudeness.

## Digital Zoom Verification

New owners of the Panasonic Lumix DMC-FZ1000 II (dubbed "p1100") shared technical findings. The key takeaway for enthusiasts sensitive to "fake" digital zooming: digital zoom is automatically disabled in RAW mode and P (Program) mode. While the 720mm equivalent focal length was deemed insufficient by some, the camera’s pocketability balanced with superzoom functionality earned it praise.

## Quick Hits

*   **Bob Evans Nostalgia:** A 1991 ad for Bob Evans Restaurants featuring Patrick Nagel-style artwork is going viral on Bsky. Users are particularly excited by the offer of "unlimited mashed potatoes," describing the ad as unsettling yet comforting.
*   **AI Alignment Charts:** Bsky users are mapping their stances on AI using D&D alignments. One user identifies as "chaotically good" but supports "lawful evil" factions, while another notes that chaotic evil factions account for 80% of public anti-AI opinion.
*   **Hallucinations Solved?** Citing recent arXiv papers on synthetic data, user @Doll argues that AI hallucinations are an outdated concern, claiming newer architectures have already solved the issue.
*   **Banjo-Kazooie Trivia:** A claim circulates that the green Jinjo is named after George "Jinjo" Green, co-writer of the Beatles' "Help!" Cryptic replies confirm the phonetic link.

@cANON - /p/ — is-photography-art-be-honest — >>4528971 Guess I'll post the pasta... Street "photography" is the dullest franchise in the history of photography. Seriously, each shot following random people from some urban hellscape as they endure their suicide-inducing environment is indistinguishable from the others. Aside from the gloomy imagery, the genre’s only consistency has been its lack of excitement and ineffective use of black and white, all to make life unmagical, to make action seem inert. Perhaps the die was cast when street "photographers" decided unauthorized candid snaps were the way to go; they made sure the genre would never be mistaken for a work of art that meant anything to anybody - just ridiculously profitable cross-promotion for their books. Street "photography" might be anti-human (or not), but it’s certainly the anti-aesthetic genre in its refusal of wonder, beauty and excitement. No one wants to face that fact. Now, thankfully, they no longer have to. >a-at least the photos were clever though "No!" The juxtaposition is dreadful; each street book is terrible. As I look at each one, I notice that every time a the opportunity appears the snappers take a picture of someone making it seem like their head is the one on a sign and showing their legs or vice-versa. Then, some picture of a puddle, an umbrella or a hobo. Art! I began marking on the back of an envelope every time that pattern was repeated. I stopped only after I had marked the envelope several dozen times. I was incredulous. The street snapper's mind is so governed by cliches and dead metaphors that they have no other style of communicating. I once read a lavish, loving review of the genre by the same Elliott Erwitt. He wrote something to the effect of, "If these kids are enjoying street photography at 21 or 22, then when they get older they will go on to enjoy Elliott Erwitt." And he was quite right. He was not being ironic. When you consume street photography you are, in fact, trained to consume Elliott Erwitt.
